title: If You’re Not Elaborating, You’re Not Listening
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This short Admired Leadership piece proposes a concrete test of listening skill: how often a listener elaborates on what others say. Elaboration means taking up the content another person offers and expanding, adding to, or developing it, whereas ignoring the comment or changing the subject reveals poor listening as a pattern. A mundane example about a colleague's spicy chicken sandwich illustrates the difference between building on a comment and moving elsewhere. The piece distinguishes lazy listeners, who merely agree, from active listeners, who add their own view to what they have heard. It closes by suggesting that elaboration may be the missing ingredient explaining why leaders who believe they listen well are not seen that way by others.
points: Elaboration, expanding on or developing the point another person has made, is offered as a practical self-test of listening quality.
Responding off-topic or shifting subjects is treated not as mere disinterest but, as a habit, as evidence of poor listening.
Merely agreeing is lazy listening; genuine elaboration adds the listener's own view or questions to the topic.
The gap between leaders' self-assessed listening and how others experience them may come down to a lack of elaboration.
quotes: When listeners elaborate, they expand, add to, or otherwise broaden or develop the conversational points being offered. Ignoring the comment, responding off-topic, or shifting to another subject indicates more than disinterest. As a pattern, it reflects poor listening.

Elaborating on what the other party has said requires taking up the content and expanding upon it. Asking questions about the sandwich, adding commentary about whether you like spicy foods, describing what you had for lunch, or inquiring about why they enjoyed it are all forms of elaboration. Suggesting it is going to rain this evening is not.
Elaboration requires focus, interest, and engagement. Most of all, it requires listening attentively to what the other person is saying and why it matters to them.

Lazy listeners expand conversations by simply agreeing or suggesting what they like about the subject. Whereas, active listeners truly elaborate on what they have heard by adding their spin or view to the topic.

It is often the case that leaders believe themselves to be excellent listeners only to learn that others don’t feel the same. It may be that elaboration or the lack of it is the missing ingredient to this competing view.
